Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
No – it’s **not a bug**.  
When a style **doesn’t contain a `glyphs` field**, MapLibre GL JS (v5.11 +​) automatically switches to its **local-font fallback mode**.  
Your `text-font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: the engine looks for a matching **web-font** (loaded with `@font-face` or `document.fonts.load()`) or a **system-installed font**. If it can’t find the name you wrote, it falls back to the browser’s generic default (usually “sans-serif” or “system UI”), which is why you see a “generic” font on the map.

So the map is working as designed; you just haven’t supplied the font that the browser can actually use.

---

## What’s really happening under the hood

| Step | What MapLibre does | Result |
|------|-------------------|--------|
| 1️⃣  | Parses the style. No `glyphs` property → **local-fonts mode** is enabled. | No request for `…/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` is made. |
| 2️⃣  | For each symbol layer it reads `text-font: ["My Fancy Font", "fallback …"]`. | The array becomes a **fallback list** just like CSS `font-family`. |
| 3️⃣  | Calls the browser’s font-resolution engine (via `document.fonts.load()` / CSS cascade). | If a font with the exact family name is already loaded (web-font or OS font), it is used. |
| 4️⃣  | If the name cannot be resolved, the browser picks its **generic fallback** (e.g. `sans-serif`). | You see the generic font on the map. |
| 5️⃣  | The text is rasterised on-device with **TinySDF** (the same SDF algorithm used for glyph-PBFs). | The label looks fine, just not in the intended typeface. |

> **Important:** This automatic fallback only exists in **MapLibre GL JS**.  
> MapLibre Native does **not** support omitting `glyphs`; it will simply fail to render the text unless you provide a `font-faces` block (or a proper `glyphs` URL).  

---

## How to get the exact font you want

You have three practical options, all of which are “expected” ways to make the style render the right typeface.

### 1️⃣ Load the font as a **web-font** (recommended for GL JS)

```html
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/MyFancyFont.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<style>
  @font-face {
    font-family: "My Fancy Font";
    src: url("/fonts/MyFancyFont.woff2") format("woff2");
    font-weight: 400;          /* match the weight you use in text-font */
    font-style: normal;
    font-display: swap;
  }
</style>
```

*Make sure the `font-family` string **exactly** matches the name you put in `text-font`.*
```json
{
  "type": "symbol",
  "layout": {
    "text-field": "{name}",
    "text-font": ["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans Regular"]
  }
}
```

If the font is hosted on a different origin, enable CORS (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your domain) so the browser can fetch it.

### 2️⃣ Use a **system-installed font**

If you control the client machines (e.g. an internal dashboard) you can install the font on the OS and reference it by its exact family name. No extra network request is needed, but the map will look different on machines that don’t have the font.

### 3️⃣ Serve **glyph-PBFs** (the classic MapLibre way)

If you prefer the original SDF-glyph pipeline (or you need the same look on MapLibre Native), add a `glyphs` URL to the style:

```json
{
  "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  ...
}
```

*You can either:*

* **Copy an existing glyph tree** (e.g. from `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/` or the `openmaptiles/fonts` repo) to your own origin, **or**
* **Generate your own** from a TTF/OTF with the Font Maker UI or `fontnik` if you have a brand-new typeface.

When `glyphs` is present, the engine will **ignore the local-font fallback** and request the PBFs for every range that appears in the map tiles.

---

## Quick checklist – why you’re seeing the generic font

| ✅ Check | What to verify |
|--------|----------------|
| **Font is actually loaded** | Open DevTools → Network → filter “font”. You should see a request for `MyFancyFont.woff2` (or `.ttf`). |
| **Family name matches** | The string in `@font-face { font-family: … }` must be identical to the first entry in `text-font`. |
| **Weight/style match** | If you use `"My Fancy Font Bold"` in `text-font`, you need a separate `@font-face` with `font-weight: 700`. |
| **CORS headers** | If the font is cross-origin, the response must include `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). |
| **No `glyphs` field** | Confirm the style truly omits `glyphs`. If you accidentally have it pointing at a dead endpoint, the engine will try the PBF route first, then fall back to local fonts **only for the ranges that fail**. |
| **Browser support** | All modern browsers support `@font-face`. Very old browsers (IE 11) may have quirks; consider using `woff` as a fallback. |

If any of the above fails, the browser falls back to its generic font, which is exactly what you’re seeing.

---

## When you *might* want to keep the generic fallback

* **Performance-first offline apps** – local-font rendering avoids a network round-trip for every Unicode range.  
* **CJK text** – MapLibre GL JS already renders Chinese/Japanese/Korean characters locally via `localIdeographFontFamily`. Supplying glyph PBFs for CJK is usually slower and unnecessary unless you need a very specific CJK typeface.

If you’re happy with the generic look for CJK but want a custom Latin font, you can combine both:

```json
{
  "layout": {
    "text-font": ["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans Regular"]
  }
}
```

CJK characters will still be drawn by the TinySDF local-ideograph path, while Latin characters will use your web-font.

---

## TL;DR – What to do next

1. **Load the font as a web-font** (or install it on the client) and make sure the name matches `text-font`.  
2. **If you need identical rendering on Native**, add a proper `glyphs` URL (or use the `font-faces` property on Native) – the local-font fallback is not available there.  
3. **Test** – open the map, inspect the network tab, and you should see the font file being fetched and no generic-font fallback warnings.

That’s all there is to it: the behavior you observed is the intended “local-fonts mode” introduced in MapLibre GL JS 5.11, not a bug. Once the correct font is available to the browser, the map will render exactly as you specified. Happy styling!

Description: anti-pattern — porting font-faces config from Native to GL JS
prompt: I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** **No.** The `font-faces` property is a **MapLibre Native-only** feature. GL JS does not understand it, and copying the block into a GL JS style will be ignored (or will cause a validation error).  

Below is a quick-reference table, then a step-by-step guide on how to get the same *offline-font* experience in GL JS, plus the pitfalls you need to watch for.

---

## 1️⃣ Why `font-faces` won’t work in GL JS

| Feature | MapLibre Native | MapLibre GL JS |
|---------|----------------|----------------|
| **`font-faces` property** | Supported (Android ≥ 11.13, iOS ≥ 6.18). Maps a `text-font` name → one or more local font files **with explicit Unicode ranges** you supply. | **Not supported** (open issue [#165](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native/issues/165)). GL JS has a completely different mechanism for “no-glyph-server” rendering. |
| **Fallback to system/web fonts** | Not automatic; you must list each file and its range in `font-faces`. | Since **v5.11.0** GL JS will *automatically* fall back to the browser’s font-resolution algorithm **if** the style has no `glyphs` URL **or** a particular glyph-range PBF fails to load. |
| **Offline-only mode** | Achieved by bundling the font files yourself and pointing `font-faces` at them. | Achieved either by (a) **omitting `glyphs` completely** and loading the fonts with normal CSS/`@font-face`, **or** (b) serving your own pre-generated glyph PBFs from a local server. |

So you cannot just copy the `font-faces` block; you must adopt one of the GL JS approaches described next.

---

## 2️⃣ Two ways to get “offline fonts” in GL JS

### A️⃣ Omit `glyphs` and use **native browser fonts** (the simplest, truly offline)

1. **Remove the `glyphs` field** from your style JSON (or set it to `null`).  
   ```json
   {
     "version": 8,
     "glyphs": null,          // <-- important
     "layers": [...]
   }
   ```

2. **Load the font files yourself** (either from the same origin or via a data-URL).  
   ```css
   @font-face {
     font-family: "MyBrand";
     src: url("./fonts/MyBrand-Regular.woff2") format("woff2");
     font-weight: 400;
     font-style: normal;
   }
   @font-face {
     font-family: "MyBrand";
     src: url("./fonts/MyBrand-Bold.woff2") format("woff2");
     font-weight: 700;
     font-style: normal;
   }
   ```

3. **Reference the font in `text-font`** exactly as you named it in `@font-face`.  
   ```json
   {
     "type": "symbol",
     "layout": {
       "text-field": "{name}",
       "text-font": ["MyBrand Regular", "MyBrand Bold", "Noto Sans Regular"]
     }
   }
   ```

4. **Result:**  
   * If the browser can load the font (offline or online), GL JS will render the text with it using TinySDF.  
   * If the font cannot be loaded, GL JS falls back to the next name in the list, eventually to the system default.  
   * No glyph-PBF server is needed, and the whole map works completely offline after the fonts have been cached.

> **Why this works:** Since v5.11.0 GL JS treats every `text-font` entry as a *CSS-style font-family* when no glyphs are available. It runs the same cascade algorithm the browser uses for normal text.

#### Gotchas

| Issue | What to watch for |
|-------|-------------------|
| **CJK characters** | GL JS always renders ideographs locally via `localIdeographFontFamily` (default `'sans-serif'`). `text-font` is ignored for those codepoints, so you cannot force a custom CJK TTF this way unless you set `localIdeographFontFamily` to a specific on-device font that you have installed (e.g., `"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif`). |
| **RTL scripts** | The fallback does **not** perform Arabic/Hebrew shaping. You still need to load the RTL text plugin: `setRTLTextPlugin(...)`. |
| **Ligature-heavy scripts (Devanagari, Khmer, etc.)** | GL JS has no shaping engine, so even with a local font you’ll see missing conjuncts. The only workaround today is to pre-render the text as images or use a different library. |
| **Weight/Style keywords** | Only the *weight* part of the `text-font` name is respected for CJK (because the glyph is generated on-device). For Latin scripts you must list each exact font-family name you want to use. |

---

### B️⃣ Serve **pre-generated glyph PBFs** from a local (or self-hosted) server

If you need **pixel-perfect glyph shapes** that match a specific font (e.g., a brand font that you cannot ship as a web-font, or you want the same look on GL JS **and** Native), you can keep a `glyphs` URL and host the `.pbf` files yourself.

1. **Generate the glyph PBFs** (once) from your TTF/OTF.  
   * Use the online **Font Maker** tool: <https://maplibre.github.io/font-maker/>  
   * Or run `fontnik` locally:  
     ```bash
     npm install -g fontnik
     fontnik --output ./fonts-pbf MyBrand-Regular.ttf
     ```
   * The output tree must be `/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. `fontstack` is the exact string you will use in `text-font` (commas for fallbacks). Example: `MyBrand%20Regular/0-255.pbf`.

2. **Host the tree** on any static server (e.g., an S3 bucket, a CDN, or a local `express` server).  
   ```js
   // Express example
   const express = require('express');
   const app = express();
   app.use('/fonts', express.static('fonts-pbf'));
   app.listen(8080);
   ```

3. **Point the style’s `glyphs` field** at that server.  
   ```json
   {
     "glyphs": "http://localhost:8080/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
     "layers": [...]
   }
   ```

4. **Keep `text-font` names** identical to the folder names you created.  
   ```json
   "layout": {
     "text-font": ["MyBrand Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"]
   }
   ```

5. **Result:**  
   * GL JS will request the appropriate PBFs for each zoom level and code-point range.  
   * Because the files are on the same origin (or CORS-enabled), the map works offline after the files have been cached.  
   * This approach works **both** in GL JS **and** Native (where you would use `font-faces` pointing at the same TTF/OTF files).  

#### Gotchas

| Issue | What to watch for |
|-------|-------------------|
| **CJK** | As before, you *usually* **don’t want** to serve CJK glyph PBFs because a single tile can trigger dozens of range requests (slow, large bandwidth). Keep `localIdeographFontFamily` at its default unless you have a very specific reason to serve them. |
| **Unicode-range matching** | GL JS will request *every* range that contains at least one codepoint used on the tile. If you split a font into multiple files (e.g., Latin vs. Cyrillic), make sure each range file covers the correct Unicode block; otherwise you’ll see “Unable to load glyph range … Rendering codepoint … locally instead.” |
| **CORS** | If you host the glyphs on a different domain, enable `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or the specific origin). Otherwise the fetch will fail and GL JS will fall back to the local-font path, which may give you a different look. |
| **Cache-busting** | When you update a font, change the URL (e.g., add a version query string) so browsers don’t keep serving stale PBFs. |

---

## 3️⃣ TL;DR – What you should do

| Goal | Recommended GL JS solution |
|------|-----------------------------|
| **Exact same offline-font behavior as Native (brand font, no internet)** | **Option B** – generate and self-host glyph PBFs, keep a `glyphs` URL. This mirrors what `font-faces` does on Native (except you don’t need to list Unicode ranges yourself; the PBFs already encode them). |
| **Simpler, truly offline, no glyph server** | **Option A** – drop `glyphs`, load the font with `@font-face` (or rely on system fonts). GL JS will render locally via TinySDF. |
| **Need CJK characters** | Keep the default `localIdeographFontFamily` (or set it to a nicer on-device CJK font). Do **not** serve CJK glyph PBFs unless you explicitly set `localIdeographFontFamily: false`. |
| **Need Arabic/Hebrew shaping** | Load the RTL plugin (`setRTLTextPlugin`) **in addition** to either Option A or B. |
| **Need Devanagari, Khmer, etc.** | Currently impossible to get correct shaping with MapLibre alone. Consider pre-rendered images or a different text-rendering library. |

---

## 4️⃣ Quick code snippets

### A) Local-font (no `glyphs`) example

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
<script type="module">
import maplibregl from 'https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@5.13.0/dist/maplibre-gl.esm.js';
import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@5.13.0/dist/maplibre-gl.esm.js';

setRTLTextPlugin(
  'https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js',
  null,
  true
);

const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: {
    version: 8,
    glyphs: null,               // <-- important
    sources: { /* … */ },
    layers: [
      {
        id: 'places',
        type: 'symbol',
        source: 'osm',
        layout: {
          'text-field': ['get', 'name'],
          'text-font': ['MyBrand Regular', 'Noto Sans Regular'],
          'text-size': 14
        }
      }
    ]
```

## 5️⃣ Bottom line

- **`font-faces` → GL JS?** No, they are unrelated mechanisms.
- **Offline fonts in GL JS?** Use either **(a) omit `glyphs` + load fonts via CSS** or **(b) self-host glyph PBFs**.
- **Keep Native & Web in sync** by generating the same glyph PBFs you would otherwise reference with `font-faces`, then point the GL JS style at those PBFs.
